entities.summary:
Flavius Aëtius (b. 390 CE, Silistra, Moesia Inferior, Roman Empire), often hailed as 'The Last of the Romans,' was a pivotal military commander and statesman of the Western Roman Empire during its tumultuous final decades. His career, spanning from the 420s until his assassination in 454 CE, was defined by his strategic genius in navigating the complex geopolitical landscape of a collapsing empire, characterized by incessant barbarian incursions and internal political strife. Aëtius's significance lies in his ability to forge shifting alliances, even with the Huns, to maintain a semblance of Roman authority in Gaul and Italy, thereby temporarily staving off the empire's complete disintegration.

The core of Aëtius's achievements revolved around his military campaigns and diplomatic maneuvering. After early life as a hostage among the Huns and Goths, he leveraged these connections to gain power. In 436 CE, he decisively defeated the Burgundians near Worms, relocating survivors to Savoy. His most celebrated triumph came in 451 CE at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains (near modern Châlons-en-Champagne), where he led a coalition of Roman and Visigothic forces, alongside other Germanic allies, to halt Attila's Hunnic invasion of Gaul. This monumental victory, though not a complete destruction of the Hunnic army, forced Attila to withdraw, saving much of Western Europe from further devastation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Aëtius is considered the last great Roman general, whose strategic leadership and military victories, particularly against Attila's Huns in 451 CE, significantly prolonged the existence of the Western Roman Empire by several decades. His career exemplifies the desperate struggle to preserve Roman authority amidst overwhelming external pressures and internal decay.
